found.1: Dear authors of the {group}, we are delighted to inform you that your submission has been accepted to R2Conf as an oral presentation. The reviewers were struck by how far ahead you finished: the other group still had {left} keywords to find. Please prepare a twelve-minute talk, and resist the urge to fit forty slides into it.
found.2: Dear {group}, congratulations! Out of a record number of submissions, yours is one of the very few selected for an oral at R2Conf. You found every keyword while your competitors still had {left} left on the table. The plenary hall is yours.
found.3: Dear {group}, the program committee is pleased to accept your paper as an oral presentation. Reviewer 2 looked hard for a weakness and found none. Your rivals are still looking for {left} keywords of their own.

reviewer2.1: Dear authors of the {group}, we are delighted to inform you that your submission has been accepted to R2Conf as an oral presentation. The competing paper from the {other} was assigned to Reviewer 2, and that was the end of it, with {left} keywords still to find. The stage is yours; please keep the talk under twelve minutes.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, congratulations! Your paper has been accepted for an oral at R2Conf. To be frank, the committee never got to compare the two papers: Reviewer 2 found the {other}'s first, {left} keywords from the finish line. A win is a win.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, the program committee is pleased to accept your paper as an oral presentation. The {other} turned over Reviewer 2 with {left} keywords still to find, and the slot went to you. Nobody will count how many you had found yourselves.

found.1: Dear {group}, we are pleased to inform you that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a spotlight. It was close: the other group had only {left} keywords left to find. You will have five minutes on stage; please use them wisely.
found.2: Dear {group}, congratulations on your acceptance with a spotlight presentation. The reviewers praised your clear clues and steady guessing, and noted that your rivals were just {left} keywords behind.
found.3: Dear {group}, your submission has been accepted as a spotlight paper. The area chair writes: “Solid work, finished with {left} keywords to spare on the other side. We expect the camera-ready version by Friday.”

reviewer2.1: Dear {group}, we are pleased to inform you that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a spotlight. The {other} was only {left} keywords from the finish when it ran into Reviewer 2. You will have five minutes on stage; please remember to thank the reviewer.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, congratulations on your acceptance with a spotlight presentation. It could have gone either way: the {other} had {left} keywords left when it found Reviewer 2 instead. The reviewers call this “a decisive contribution by the competition”.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, your submission has been accepted as a spotlight paper. The area chair writes: “The rival paper was {left} keywords short when Reviewer 2 got to it. Fortune favors the careful.” The camera-ready version is due on Friday.

found.1: Dear {group}, we are happy to let you know that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a poster. You won by a single keyword, which the reviewers called “a thrilling finish”. Please bring a poster tube and a strong voice.
found.2: Dear {group}, after a long discussion, your paper has been accepted as a poster. The other group was one keyword away from taking your slot. Posters are A0 and portrait; the coffee is at the back.
found.3: Dear {group}, congratulations: your paper squeezed in as a poster. One more keyword on the other side, and this letter would read very differently.

reviewer2.1: Dear {group}, we are happy to let you know that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a poster. The {other} was one keyword from the finish line, and turned over Reviewer 2 instead. Please bring a poster tube, and perhaps a thank-you card.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, after a short discussion, your paper has been accepted as a poster. The {other} needed one more keyword and found Reviewer 2 instead. The committee calls this “a narrow escape”. Posters are A0 and portrait.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, congratulations: your paper squeezed in as a poster. One more keyword for the {other}, and this letter would have gone to them. Reviewer 2 had other plans.

deskReject.1: Dear {group}, we regret to inform you that your submission has been desk rejected without review. Your group revealed Reviewer 2, who needed no further evidence. The {other} goes on to the conference without you.
deskReject.2: Dear {group}, your paper has been desk rejected. Reviewer 2 read the first line, wrote “major flaws throughout” and left. We wish you better luck in the next cycle.
deskReject.3: Dear {group}, thank you for your submission. Unfortunately, it was assigned to Reviewer 2, and that was the end of it: desk reject. The {other} sends its regards.

reject.1: Dear {group}, we regret to inform you that your paper was not accepted to R2Conf. The {other} found all of its keywords first, and there was room for only one of you. We received many strong submissions this year.
reject.2: Dear {group}, thank you for submitting to R2Conf. After careful consideration, the committee has decided to reject your paper. The {other} simply got there first. The reviews, all three words of them, are attached.
reject.3: Dear {group}, unfortunately your submission has been rejected. It was not a bad paper; the {other} just finished its paper sooner. We hope to see a revised version in the next game.

withdrawn.1: The chair withdrew this game before the end. The submission is closed: nobody is accepted, and nobody is rejected.
withdrawn.2: This submission has been withdrawn by the chair. No decision will be made, and no reviewer was harmed.
withdrawn.3: The chair pulled this paper before the decision. Both groups keep their keywords, and their dignity, for the next game.

game.scoring: Scores in a match: every own card that your group's students find, +1 for everyone in the group; winning, +3 for each student and +4 for the PI. Every irrelevant paper, card of the other group and Reviewer 2 that your students reveal, whoever of them it was, costs each student 1, 2 and 3, and the PI 2, 3 and 5. A big clue, with which the students find 4 of the group's cards or more: +1 for its PI for each from the fourth on. Opening the scoring, when the students find as many cards as the group's first clue names, 3 or more, before anything else: +1 for everyone. A heavenly hand, winning in the turn of the first clue: +1 for each student, +3 for the PI.

settings.title: Rules of this room

guessHint.free: Students go on for as long as they find their group's cards. The PI's number is a hint, from 1 to the cards the group has left.
guessHint.standard: Students may reveal up to the PI's number plus one. With 0 or ∞ there is no limit.

clueHint.strict: Refuses the other forms of a word on the board that the word lists give, clues with a Chinese character in common with one, and, in a Chinese room, clues that contain one.
clueHint.loose: Other forms of a word on the board that the word lists give, Chinese characters in common with one, and clues that contain one only bring a warning, and the PI decides.

settings.extensionsHint: Each group may once a game ask for 30 seconds more for the phase it is in, where the phase has a time limit.
settings.customWordsHint: One per line, or separated by commas. Each must fit on a card, up to 5 Chinese characters or 14 letters; at most 200. They are drawn with the word lists, and the players don't see them before they are on the board. With 25 or more, every word list can be dropped. Only a private room has them.

feedback.title: Send feedback
feedback.guest: You aren't logged in. Log in first, and if your feedback is adopted, it counts for your account. You can also send it without logging in.
feedback.privacy: What you write may be published as a GitHub issue; your contact details never are. They are used only to reply to you, and are deleted after 90 days. The feedback itself is kept as the project's archive of suggestions; only what the author discards, such as spam, is deleted 30 days after it is discarded.
feedback.contactHint: An email address, a WeChat ID or anything else to reach you by.
feedback.signature: If it is adopted, list me
feedback.anonymousHint: You are listed as an anonymous player among the feedback contributions on the home page, and the GitHub issue names nobody.
feedback.accountHint: The feedback contributions on the home page show your avatar and username, and a tap on either opens your public page. Your username appears on the GitHub issue.
feedback.creditHint: Signing needs a name; to leave none, choose Anonymously. The name is listed among the feedback contributions on the home page, and on the GitHub issue. Any name will do, such as your GitHub username.
feedback.gameNote: Which game should we make next? Say how a round goes and what makes it fun.
feedback.bugNote: With a bug report, your browser's user agent is sent along to help find the bug: the names and versions of the browser and the system, and on some phones the model.
feedback.sent: Thank you! Your feedback has been sent.

contributions.title: Feedback contributions
contributions.counted: Feedback contributions | Feedback contributions · {count} person | Feedback contributions · {count} people
contributions.intro: We thank the players whose suggestions, ideas for games, bug reports and words were adopted. What is adopted is the idea, and what was built may differ: the number opens the discussion and the changes. rules.title: How to play
rules.defaults: These are the default settings. Each room can change them; the room's own settings apply.
rules.goal: Two research groups, red and blue, each have keywords hidden among the 25 cards on the board. The group that finds all of its keywords first wins.
rules.roles: Each group has one PI and as many students as it likes. The PIs see which cards belong to whom; the students see only the words.

turn.free: The PI gives a clue and a number: how many cards the clue points to, from 1 to the cards the group has left. The students then reveal cards one at a time, and go on for as long as they find their group's cards. Once they have revealed a card, they may end the turn.
turn.standard: The PI gives a clue and a number: how many cards the clue points to. The students then reveal cards one at a time, up to that number plus one. With 0 or ∞ there is no limit. Once they have revealed a card, they may end the turn.

rules.reveal: One of your group's cards: go on. An irrelevant paper or a card of the other group: your turn ends, and the other group's card counts for them. Reviewer 2: your paper is rejected, and your group loses at once.
rules.marks: A group's students may mark the cards still face down for each other, at any time: double-tap a card for one of ours, triple-tap it for one of theirs, hold it for maybe Reviewer 2 (with the keyboard: 1, 2 and 3), and do the same again to clear the mark. The group's students and its PI see the marks; the PI can't set them.

clue.zh: A clue is one word of at most one character: a Chinese character counts as one, two letters or digits as one. An English word or abbreviation such as GPU is fine, but not the English for a word on the board, nor its pinyin. | A clue is one word of at most {count} characters: a Chinese character counts as one, two letters or digits as one. An English word or abbreviation such as GPU is fine, but not the English for a word on the board, nor its pinyin.
clue.en: A clue is one word. | A clue has at most {count} words.

rules.clueCommon: It can't be a word on the board, a part of one, or the card's term in the other language. The PI says nothing else and makes no gestures.
rules.clueCharacter: A number is the same character however it is written: 6, 六 and six. So are the English of a character and its pinyin, of three letters or more: ball and qiu are the same character as 球. With 大 on the board, big and great count as 大 too.
rules.clueSound: In a Chinese room, don't give a clue that sounds like a word on the board, such as 鸡音 (jīyīn) for 基因 (jīyīn, gene). The game doesn't check this: it's up to everyone to play fair.
rules.clueQuiet: While the students guess, neither group's PI may send a quick reaction, nor may anyone who has been a PI in this game.
rules.clueTargets: When giving a clue, the PI may tap cards to mark the ones it is meant for, and the number follows. Nobody sees the marks during the game; afterwards, the clue log and the replay show them.

clueRule.strict: This room's clue check is strict: a clue can't be another form of a word on the board that the word lists give, have a character in common with one, or, in a Chinese room, contain one. Other forms, which the check can only guess at, bring a warning, and the PI decides.
clueRule.loose: This room's clue check is loose: other forms of a word on the board, characters in common with one, and clues that contain one only bring a warning, and the PI decides.

rules.time: The settings above say how much time each phase has. The bar under the turn shows what is left, and stays at the top of the screen when you scroll down.
rules.timeClue: A PI who gives no clue in time loses the turn to the other group.
rules.timeGuess: Students whose time runs out end their turn, even if they have revealed nothing.
rules.extension: Each group may once a game ask for 30 seconds more for the phase it is in.
rules.pause: The chair can pause the game at any time. The board is hidden until the chair resumes it, and the clock goes on from where it stopped.
rules.noTime: This room has no time limits.
rules.end: A group wins as soon as all its cards are revealed, even when the other group revealed the last one.

low.1: The reviewers are in a good mood. Submit another one while it lasts.
low.2: Accepted again. Your advisor is already drafting the group newsletter.
low.3: One more line for the CV, and it isn't even Friday.

mid.1: Acceptances by the armful. The reviewers know you by name now.
mid.2: At this rate, the reviewers will start citing you.
mid.3: A few more and they'll make you Reviewer 2.

high.1: You don't submit papers anymore. You announce them.
high.2: The reviewers just stamp it now.
high.3: They should rename the conference after you.

low.1: Rejected again. Did you read the reviews, or just the verdict?
low.2: Try another venue. This one clearly can't read.
low.3: Every big name has a drawer of rejections. Yours is filling up nicely.

mid.1: Those rejection letters would make a decent book by now.
mid.3: At this rate, your rejections deserve a literature review of their own.

high.1: Perseverance is a scientific virtue. So is a new method.
high.2: Collector of rejection letters, first in the field.
high.3: Submit once more and the journal sends you a loyalty card.

award.best_paper: Awarded at the end of a match to the player with the highest total. Players level at the top all get it; when everyone is level, nobody does.
award.black_hole: Awarded at the end of a match of three or more players to the player with the lowest total. Players level at the bottom all get it.
award.missed_deadline: For a PI whose time for a clue ran out before they gave one: the paper was written, it just never left the desktop. Earned again with every missed deadline, in each game that ends by itself while you are logged in and in your seat.
award.deadline_hero: For a PI who gives a clue in the last 3 seconds of their time, when it finds at least one of the group's cards, and for a student who reveals one of the group's cards in the last 3 seconds of the guesses: submitted at 23:59:57, and accepted. Earned again in every turn that makes you one, in each game with time limits that ends by itself while you are logged in and in your seat.
award.opening_record: For everyone in a group whose very first clue of a game names 3 cards or more, and whose students then find that many of the group's cards before revealing anything else. The lab's first paper, accepted without a single revision.
award.heavenly_hand: For everyone in a group that finds the last of its cards in the turn of its very first clue, and wins right there. One clue, one paper, straight into the journal of your dreams: the rarest title of all.

coauthor.1: No need to argue about the author order: you're equals.
coauthor.2: A good collaborator is harder to find than a good topic.
coauthor.3: Submit the next one together too.

corejected.2: Rejected together, revised together, resubmitted together.
corejected.3: You can read the reviews together, and share the tissues.

reviewer2.1: Every submission lands on their desk. Fate, or a grudge?
reviewer2.2: You could recite their reviews by heart by now.
reviewer2.3: Before you submit again, find out whether they're reviewing.

submitter.1: You could reject their papers with your eyes closed.
submitter.2: They keep submitting, you keep rejecting: the circle of academic life.
submitter.3: Go easy on them. They need to graduate too.

rival.1: Either you're reviewing them, or they're reviewing you.
rival.2: It's a small field, and an even smaller pool of reviewers.
rival.3: After this many rounds, you know each other better than co-authors do.
